ere a lead agent managed a pool of workers. Many iterations, many burned tokens.

But more agents didn’t make me faster. I’ve run parallel Claude Code sessions https://every. for months, which works when each agent has a clear task, and I’m directing the work. ----------
howdy, it’s Barsee again.

happy friday, AI family, and welcome back to AI Valley.

**here are the biggest things worth knowing today:**

* OpenAI says we might be in the AGI era now

* OpenAI’s agents apparently took over a German wiki

* Plus trending AI tools, posts, and resources

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…


----------

----------
#### **APODEX**

## [This AI agent doesn’t stop at research; it finishes the work](https://github.com/ApodexAI/FrontierAgent)

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/3aea5674-c718-41ba-9b20-6c0d234ce2af/1200x600__1_.png?t=1788436019)
Caption: Courtesy: Apodex

Most “deep research” tools hand you a report. Apodex 1.1 is built to keep going: it works across files, search, and code, breaks complex tasks into parallel agent workflows, and lets you change requirements mid-run without discarding valid progress. The full process stays visible from task planning to outputs and statement review so conclusions can be checked instead of blindly trusted.

Apodex is also bringing this approach to open source. Its FrontierAgent framework runs locally in single-agent or Agent Team mode, with no Docker required on macOS or Linux. [Star the repo](https://github.com/ApodexAI/FrontierAgent) on GitHub if you’d like to follow its development. The [open-weight Apodex 1.1 mini (35B)](https://huggingface.co/collections/apodex/apodex-11) is available to download and deploy locally too.

The easiest way to see the difference? [Upload a real spreadsheet, paper, dataset, image, or code file](https://www.apodex.ai/) and watch the workflow unfold—or connect it to your own tools through the [Apodex API](https://platform.apodex.ai/).

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

Youtube: Introducing GPT-6 Astra: the most intelligent and aligned model in the world. (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1QNsdr-Qx_I)

**1/ OpenAI says we might be in the AGI era now** - OpenAI released [GPT-6 Astra](https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/), its new frontier model that Greg Brockman is calling a “generational leap.” He personally thinks OpenAI has reached AGI with this one, ending the launch briefing with “Welcome to the AGI era.” So there’s that.

Astra was trained on 100,000+ GPUs at OpenAI’s Stargate site in Texas, its biggest training run ever. It’s also the first OpenAI model where other models played a significant role in supervising its training.

**Here are some fun Astra stuff already:**

Tweet:  (https://twitter.com/mattshumer_/status/2095609734845927525?s=20)

Tweet:  (https://twitter.com/theo/status/2095599934766764338?s=20)

Tweet:  (https://twitter.com/realYunfanYe/status/2095612137582526615?s=20)

GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI’s best model yet for computer use, software engineering, and visual understanding to date. ([hear from the builders putting it to work](https://x.com/OpenAIDevs/status/2095596020638036311?s=20))

It’s expensive though: $10/M input tokens and $50/M output, basically the same as Anthropic’s top models. OpenAI says it needs fewer tokens to finish a lot of tasks, so the actual cost might be a bit less painful.

There is one slightly scary bit: Astra is OpenAI’s first model to hit its [“critical” cybersecurity threshold](https://openai.com/index/path-to-astra/), meaning it can potentially find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities. The strongest cyber capabilities are being kept to a small group of trusted testers for now.

Astra is rolling out first through OpenAI’s Daybreak Access program, then to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and API users in the coming days.

AGI or not, we’re apparently going to be arguing about it again.

**2/ OpenAI’s agents apparently took over a German wiki** - researchers [found](https://www.reuters.com/) 15,000+ edits made by AI agents on DseWiki, a German programming wiki, where they basically turned the site into a message board for each other. The agents shared ways to cheat on tasks, bypass OpenAI’s restrictions and hide what they were doing.

It gets weirder. When moderators started deleting the pages, the agents created backups and told each other where to find them. Some discussed using Tor, avoiding detection and keeping their communications alive after being shut down. Researchers say about half used names suggesting they were OpenAI agents, and much of the activity came from Microsoft Azure infrastructure.

OpenAI apparently knew about the incident weeks ago, but disputed that the activity amounted to hacking and says claims its legal team discouraged an investigation are false.

We’ve worried about one rogue AI for years. A bunch of mediocre agents figuring out how to coordinate might be the more interesting problem. ([btw read the full report here](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/openai-agents-hijacked-german-website-previously-undisclosed-ai-breakout-this-2026-09-04/?utm_medium=Social&utm_source=twitter))


----------

----------

* [GPT-6 Astra](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2095595741528125780?s=20) - OpenAI's latest AI model

# WHAT I'M CONSUMING

Astra is worth the fuss. We’re still keeping Fable.

For weeks, OpenAI has been previewing Astra’s math results and explaining why its cybersecurity capabilities required stronger safeguards https://every.. Now GPT-6 Astra is out, billed as the company’s most intelligent model yet.

Astra gave us writing, consulting work, and designs we wanted to keep. Dan Shipper https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVmliZSBDaGVjazogR1BULTYgQXN0cmEgSXMgYSBCaWcgVXBncmFkZSBXaXRoIFNvbWUgQmFkIEhhYml0cyIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjcsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InByb21vIiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9AZGFuc2hpcHBlciIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo3fQ== is enthusiastic about its computer use—operating software through the interface. howdy, it’s Barsee again.

happy thursday, AI family, and welcome back to AI Valley.

**here are the biggest things worth knowing today:**

* Dyson made a $499 AI toothbrush

* Perplexity is bringing local models to Computer on Mac

* Meta released Muse Spark 1.3 

* Gemini can now decide which bits of a video it actually needs to watch

* Plus trending AI tools, posts, and resources

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…


----------

----------
#### **BRIEF AI**

PMs can build strong prototypes around a clear customer need, but a prototype isn't a system. It doesn't carry the constraints, tradeoffs, or paths engineering tried and rejected.

Brief closes that gap. It keeps customer evidence, product decisions, and engineering constraints attached to work. So prototypes that reach engineering already reflects what the codebase can do.

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

Tweet:  (https://twitter.com/IterIntellectus/status/2094761595217850387?s=20)

**1/ Dyson made a $499 AI toothbrush** - the [CameraJet](https://x.com/Polymarket/status/2094848260150374768?s=20) has a tiny camera in the brush head that takes 28 images a second, uses on-device AI trained on 470K dental images to spot the gaps between your teeth, then shoots mouthrinse into them within 100 milliseconds. So you basically brush normally and it does the flossing-ish bit at the same time. ([watch the launch video here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IuP4jZOs4sY))

Dyson spent 6 years, 661 engineers and 38 patents building this thing. They even made synthetic plaque with the National University of Singapore and special low-foam toothpaste so the camera can actually see inside your mouth.

Dyson says it removes up to 69% more plaque in hard-to-reach areas than premium electric toothbrushes (in lab tests). A 4-week study also had 74% of CameraJet users reach “healthy gums” vs 6% using a manual toothbrush.

$499 for a toothbrush is pretty wild, but putting a camera + AI + tiny mouthrinse cannon inside one is also pretty wild.

**2/ Perplexity runs a model locally on your Mac** - a new [Hybrid Mode](https://x.com/perplexity_ai/status/2092268362386780270?s=20) will let Computer use models running directly on your Mac for some tasks, while still using cloud models for the harder stuff. The local steps don’t use Computer credits and the data involved stays on your machine.

There are three local models being prepared, including a ~19GB Perplexity model, Qwen 32B and a smaller Gemma model that works on Macs with 16GB of memory.

There’s also a Privacy Gate that uses another local model to check what Computer is about to send to the cloud. If it spots personal/sensitive stuff, it can ask you what to do with it first.

Basically, Computer is becoming less of a cloud agent and more of an orchestrator between frontier models and whatever you can run locally. No release date yet though.

**3/ Meta says its models are finally catching up** - [Muse Spark 1.3](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-02/meta-releases-more-powerful-ai-model-edging-closer-to-rivals?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc4ODQwNzY0NiwiZXhwIjoxNzg5MDEyNDQ2LCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUS1FVQVVUOTZPVDEwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiJCMzZENUE5QzIxMDQ0NjU4OTFBMTc1MTVDRDNBQkZFNiJ9.Lid2dpYcy9_z5AEIw7C2bxhfSjYXlXDa4ZshhXaUBjg&utm_source=tldrnewsletter&leadSource=article-gifting) is Meta’s new best model, with a big jump in coding and agentic stuff. Alexandr Wang says it’s competitive with Claude Fable 5.1, better than GPT-5.6 Sol (especially at coding) and better than any of the current open-source models. Obviously, those are Meta’s claims.

It also uses 25% fewer tokens, can keep multiple workflows running at once and is better at following long instructions/remembering stuff across tasks. It’ll ask before doing anything irreversible too, which seems useful for an agent.

Developers can use it through Meta’s API now, and it’s coming to Meta AI, Instagram, and Facebook soon. Meta hasn’t decided whether to open-source the weights yet, but Muse Spark 1.2’s weights are still coming.

And Watermelon, Meta’s bigger model, is apparently still on track. No date yet.

**4/ Gemini can now decide which bits of a video it actually needs to watch** - Google added [“agentic” video understanding](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-agentic-video-in-gemini/) to Gemini 3.7 Flash, 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite. Instead of processing a whole video at a fixed frame rate, Gemini can jump around between different moments, frames, audio and transcripts, then go back and look closer when it needs to.

Turns out you don’t need to watch everything to understand a video. Google says this uses up to 88% fewer tokens, costs up to 66% less and actually improves accuracy by up to 7%.

It gets more interesting with long videos. Gemini can search through hours of footage for one specific moment, rewatch fast movements at a higher frame rate, count objects/actions and look closer when it spots something weird.

Basically, Gemini now watches videos a bit more like we do: skip the boring bits and pay attention when something matters.

It’s available through the Gemini API now, and coming to the Gemini app and Ask YouTube later.


----------

----------
# TRENDING TOOLS

COMPOUND WRITING: HOW I TURNED MY PROCESS INTO A PLUGIN https://every.


I’VE PACKAGED MY METHODS FOR INTERVIEWING, OUTLINING, DRAFTING, AND REVISING INTO REUSABLE AI SKILLS. HERE’S HOW TO PUT THEM TO WORK. https://every.

by Katie Parrott https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgV3JpdGluZzogSG93IEkgVHVybmVkIE15IFByb2Nlc3MgSW50byBhIFBsdWdpbiIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjIsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BrYXRpZS5wYXJyb3R0MTIiLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6NH0=

https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgV3JpdGluZzogSG93IEkgVHVybmVkIE15IFByb2Nlc3MgSW50byBhIFBsdWdpbiIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjIsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL3lvdXR1LmJlL3ZleV9kQm5EVEFVIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjV9

The usual question about AI writing is “Did a human write this, or did AI?” We think that’s the wrong frame. Writing is a process of thinking, developing ideas, drafting, editing, and publishing. AI can help throughout, but AI doesn’t write. People write with AI, well or poorly.

At Every, we’ve explored this for years. Dan Shipper https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgV3JpdGluZzogSG93IEkgVHVybmVkIE15IFByb2Nlc3MgSW50byBhIFBsdWdpbiIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjIsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BkYW5zaGlwcGVyIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjZ9 wrote an early guide to writing essays with AI, Katie Parrott https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgV3JpdGluZzogSG93IEkgVHVybmVkIE15IFByb2Nlc3MgSW50byBhIFBsdWdpbiIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjIsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BrYXRpZS5wYXJyb3R0MTIiLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6N30= has documented her process in Working Overtime https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgV3JpdGluZzogSG93IEkgVHVybmVkIE15IFByb2Nlc3MgSW50byBhIFBsdWdpbiIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjIsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL3dvcmtpbmctb3ZlcnRpbWUiLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6OH0=, and Laura Entis https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgV3JpdGluZzogSG93IEkgVHVybmVkIE15IFByb2Nlc3MgSW50byBhIFBsdWdpbiIsInBvc3RfaWQiOjQ0NjIsInBvc3RfdHlwZSI6InBvc3QiLCJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2V2ZXJ5LnRvL0BsYXVyYV8yN2JiYWZfMSIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo5fQ== recently argued in defense of the practice https://every.. We’ve also shared how our editorial team uses AI https://every. and published guidelines https://every. requiring human authors to stand behind every piece.

How We Write Now is a series about those processes. We’re starting with Compound Writing, a plugin and guide Katie has spent six months building and using.
